title: The head, the pillar, the peak
hook: Mu'adh asks what leads to the garden, and is told of worship, the doors of good, and to guard his tongue
tomorrow: some things Allah left unsaid, on purpose. how is that mercy?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the farewell admonition: a talk that made eyes weep, and one grip to keep. Hold it with your molars. Today, a question asked on the road.
screen: `HOLD IT WITH YOUR MOLARS.` → `A QUESTION ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: The reply is already typed. Three lines, every word true, sharp enough to end something. A thumb hovers over send. Now a road in Arabia, long ago. A young man named Mu'adh ibn Jabal is traveling with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and one morning he comes up close and asks a huge question: tell me a deed that brings me into the garden and keeps me from the Fire. The Prophet says: you've asked about something great, and it's easy for the one Allah makes it easy for. Then he starts to build.
screen: `A THUMB OVER SEND.` → `MU'ADH ON THE ROAD.` → `A HUGE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: First the ground floor: worship Allah and join nothing to Him, pray, give zakah, fast Ramadan, make the pilgrimage. Then the doors of good: fasting is a shield, charity puts out a sin the way water puts out fire, and prayer in the middle of the night. Then a picture, in paraphrase from Tirmidhi's collection: shall I tell you the head of the whole matter, its pillar, and its peak? The head is Islam. The pillar is prayer. The peak is jihad, striving in Allah's path. A whole building, top to bottom. And here's the twist. He asks: shall I tell you what holds all of that together? And he takes hold of his own tongue and says: restrain this. Mu'adh is honestly surprised. Will we really be held to account for what we say? The answer comes back as a question: what throws people on their faces into the Fire, if not the harvest of their tongues? That's the detail to tell a friend tonight. After the head, the pillar and the peak, the Prophet points at something small enough to fit behind the teeth. And a harvest is what you planted, one careless word at a time, without noticing each one was a seed.
screen: `THE GROUND FLOOR AND THE DOORS.` · `HEAD, PILLAR, PEAK.` · `HE TAKES HOLD OF HIS TONGUE.` · `THE HARVEST OF THE TONGUE.` · then, large: `GUARD THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Rest the tip of your tongue lightly behind your top teeth and let your jaw go soft. For the sit, each time a sentence starts to form, notice it arrive, and let it stay unsaid for now. Nothing is being silenced forever; you're just watching the seeds before they're planted.
The head. In the Prophet's picture, the head of the matter is Islam, the pillar is prayer, the peak is striving. And the tongue holds all of it.
Hold onto this: guard the tongue, the small key to a big building. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1457 COUNTS.` → `HADITH 29 OF 42 · YEAR FIVE, 31 OF 365.` → `TOMORROW: SOME THINGS ALLAH LEFT UNSAID, ON PURPOSE. HOW IS THAT MERCY?`

howItsDone: Muslims who study al-Nawawi's forty learn this hadith as a summary of the faith: the pillars first, then voluntary fasting, charity and night prayer, with guarding the tongue as what keeps it all safe.

the hadith is about the harvest of careless words, not about staying silent when speech is needed.

fork.setup: you had a solid week: on time, helpful at home, kind at school. on the ride home you tear into a cousin, in detail. what does Mu'adh's hadith say about the week?
options: a good week outweighs one rant; deeds count more than words.
the words are part of the harvest too; the tongue can tip the building.
it doesn't count if everything you said was true.
fork.reveal: after the head, the pillar and the peak, the Prophet held his tongue: restrain this. what throws people on their faces is the harvest of their tongues.

original.note: Arabic: the head of the matter is Islam. the first part of the Prophet's picture for Mu'adh.

what a scholar hears: the doors of good, the head, pillar and peak, then the turn: restrain this, and the harvest of the tongues.

chat.says: back at school. council chat: someone joked Leo's family 'should've bought a boat.' i typed a PARAGRAPH. send?
options: Hold it. Tell him privately, in one plain line, that it hurt. Words are a harvest.
Send it. Guarding your tongue is about lying, and every word you wrote is true.
Leave the chat. Guarding your tongue means staying out of every hard conversation.
chat.meaning: In Mu'adh's hadith the tongue holds the whole building. True words can still be a bad harvest; say less, and say it well.

Mu'adh ibn Jabal.meaning: a young companion of the Prophet, known for his learning

zakah.meaning: the required yearly charity, one of the pillars

jihad.meaning: striving; here, striving in Allah's path

Tirmidhi.meaning: a scholar whose hadith collection records this conversation

sources.ref: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 2616 (Mu'adh ibn Jabal: the head of the matter, its pillar and its peak; the harvest of the tongues)
